sweep_summary: Three title hits for Giryama (giry1241; catalog: fixed-unreviewed, penultimate 'tonic accent' per Taylor 1891). None is open. (1) Philippson 1991 doctoral thesis (542 pp, French, Paris 5) — comparative typology of tone vs. penultimate accent across c. 50 East African Bantu languages incl. Giryama; only the theses.fr abstract is reachable ('accessible: non', no HAL deposit, no Google Books preview); print-only via Sudoc; HIGH priority to acquire. (2) Philippson 2005 'Pitch accent in Comorian and Proto-Sabaki tones' (RMCA festschrift, pp. 199-220) — Google Books snippets (pp. 199, 219) show it uses Giryama tonal phrasing data to reconstruct Proto-Sabaki tones and derive Comorian pitch accent; tone-comparative, silent on stress placement in the snippets; snippet-only, no DOI/open copy; medium priority. (3) Rassner 1980 UW-Madison PhD 'Narrative rhythms of Giryama ngano' (2 vols, 381 leaves) — oral-literature study of narrative rhythm/scansion (Aristoxenus, Saintsbury, Boas, Lévi-Strauss per snippets), not word stress; priority none. Search engines (Bing/DDG/Brave/Mojeek/Qwant/Startpage), OpenAlex, Semantic Scholar, HathiTrust, HAL file downloads and Google Books HTML were all blocked or rate-limited from our machine; the Google Books Atom feed, theses.fr API, Crossref, HAL metadata API and Glottolog worked. Bonus statement read (snippet, not a sweep item): Nurse & Hinnebusch 1993 'Swahili and Sabaki' (section 'Tone (Stress) in Sabaki' by Philippson): in Mijikenda 'the penultimate syllable is always quite prominent, this prominence is due to length only, pitch contrasts being assigned distinctively' — consistent with and refining the catalog's fixed-penultimate coding (predictable penultimate length + distinctive tone, no stress accent); page not obtained, so it does not yet supersede Taylor 1891. Recommended acquisitions: Philippson 1991 (Sudoc print) and the Philippson tone/stress section of Nurse & Hinnebusch 1993 (library print), plus the already-flagged Volk 2007/2011. new_statements.reading: In Mijikenda (of which Giryama is the largest variety) the penultimate syllable is always prominent, but that prominence is penultimate LENGTH only; pitch is distinctive (tone). This is consistent with the catalog's fixed-penultimate coding (Taylor 1891's 'tonic accent on the last syllable but one') and refines it: the fixed penultimate prominence is predictable lengthening, not a stress accent, and the language is tonal — matching what the held Volk 2011 BLS paper says ('the penult is predictably lengthened'). It is a group-level (Mijikenda) statement read only as a snippet without a page number.

audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: the deciding quotation (Taylor 1891, Introduction p. xiii, secs. 3 'Tonic Accent' and 4 'Stress Accent', including both listed exceptions) is present verbatim in the held scanned file at lines 733-755 under the p. xiii running head. (2) Deciding source: an 1891 missionary vocabulary with a short grammatical introduction — impressionistic, and it predates recognition that Giryama is a tone language. It is not the best available description: Glottolog lists Volk 2007 (MA, Giryama tonology, 82 pp) and the held Hyman papers cite Volk 2011 (PhD, Mijikenda tonology); neither is held. However, held modern material corroborates the coding: Volk 2011 BLS 37 p. 389 (Giryama): 'Vowel length is not contrastive; the penult is predictably lengthened'; p. 397: the phrase-final syllable is never high; Hyman & Leben 2017 (held) show Giryama /H/ surfacing on the phrase-pen

sources.quote: This work studies the very diverse prosodic systems of east African bantu languages, on the basis of non-linear (autosegmental and metrical) phonology. We find a one end purely tonal systems (like kikuyu) and at the other end systems with purely demarcative penultimate stress, with all intermediate cases. [...] a hypothesis is presented according to which the emergence of penultimate accent is the main cause of the evolution of these systems.
sources.locator: theses.fr record, FR and EN abstracts; 'accessible':'non' (no online full text; Sudoc print only)
sources.note: Comparative typology of tone vs. accent across c. 50 East African Bantu languages; Glottolog codes it for Giryama [nyf] (and Digo, Chonyi-Dzihana-Kauma, Pokomo, Swahili, Comorian etc.). The abstract (FR: 'depuis des langues pleinement tonales (kikuyu) jusqu'à des langues à accent démarcatif pénultième (swahili)') places languages on a tone-to-penultimate-accent continuum and argues the rise of a demarcative penultimate accent drove the evolution; it names no Giryama-specific fact. Full text not online: theses.fr 'accessible: non', not in HAL (13 Philippson deposits checked), Google Books id 8…
